# SK3510 — A variable already owned by `using` is disposed again

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`Dispose()` is called by hand on a variable whose `using` disposes it at the end of the scope anyway.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Lifetime |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

A `using` disposes its resource when the scope ends, on every path including the exceptional one, so an explicit `Dispose()` on the same variable is a second call that the language guarantees will happen. Double disposal is only harmless for a type whose `Dispose` is idempotent — the framework asks for that and not every type delivers it, and a second call that releases a handle number the process has since reissued corrupts an unrelated file rather than throwing. Deleting the call removes the second disposal without changing when the first one happens.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
void Copy(string path) {
    using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
    Read(stream);
    stream.Dispose();
}
```

Write:

```csharp
void Copy(string path) {
    using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
    Read(stream);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Which object the `using` disposes is a language guarantee rather than an analysis.** A `using` variable is read-only, so nothing between the declaration and the explicit call can have made the two disposals land on different objects; the rule does not have to prove it. ⚠ Ownership is read from the variable's own declarator, never from an enclosing `using` that happens to name the same identifier — a shadowing local of the same name in an inner scope is a different symbol and is not reported. ⚠ The call must be an entire statement directly inside a block: `if (failed) reader.Dispose();` is the same redundancy and is not reported, because deleting the statement would leave an `if` with no body, and a fix that produces text which does not parse is the one failure a fixing tool may not have. A `Dispose()` whose result is read, or one behind an `&&`, has nothing the fix can remove. ⚠ The invoked member is resolved by the semantic model and must be the parameterless disposal contract the `using` will itself invoke — `Dispose` is an ordinary identifier and a type may declare one that does something else. `Close()` is not reported: it is a different method, it is not always an alias for `Dispose`, and deleting it is not the same edit. A call reached across a lambda or a local function is skipped, because when that body runs is not something the enclosing `using` says anything about. ⚠ **#425: the language guarantee covers which object is disposed, not when or by which method.** #412's audit measured three ways the deleted call was not the one the `using` makes. The call must be the last thing the scope does — the last statement of its block and of every block out to the `using`'s scope, followed at most by a `return` of a literal or of another local, with no `using` declared later in the scope — because an explicit `Dispose` earlier flushes what the next statement reads (`'hello'` → `''`). `DisposeAsync` is matched only on an `await using` and `Dispose` only on a plain one, since a plain `using` never calls `DisposeAsync`. And the called method must be the interface member the `using` calls, so a public `Dispose` beside an explicit `IDisposable.Dispose` is not reported.
